draft:
Walmart, the US retail giant, has emerged as a key player in the debate over religious freedom laws in several states. The company, which employs over 50,000 people in Arkansas, has come out strongly against a religious freedom law in its home state, warning that it would allow discrimination against gay and lesbian customers. Walmart's opposition to the law has resonated with many, including Apple CEO Tim Cook and the head of the NCAA. The company's stance is seen as a reflection of its diverse consumer base and the country's increasingly progressive views on gay equality.

Walmart's actions have been praised by some prominent Republicans, including former Minnesota Gov. Tim Pawlenty, who has urged the party to take a more inclusive stance on issues such as the minimum wage and discrimination against gay and lesbians. Pawlenty noted that Walmart's actions "foreshadow where the Republican Party will need to move."

The debate has reached presidential politics, with likely GOP candidate Jeb Bush moderating his tone on the issue and Sen. Ted Cruz digging in. Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton has also weighed in, calling on Arkansas Gov. Asa Hutchinson to veto the bill.

The backlash over the religious freedom measures in Indiana and Arkansas has highlighted the business community's overwhelming support for workplace policies that promote gay equality. CEOs of companies big and small have spoken out against the laws, with many threatening to pull out of the states. The Human Rights Campaign has praised the business community for standing up for equality and against discrimination.

Easter is a significant event in the Christian faith, celebrating the completion of Christ's mission of salvation through his Crucifixion and Resurrection. However, the holiday has also picked up peripheral trappings, such as the Easter bunny and colorful eggs, which have origins in paganism and European customs. 

The date of Easter is determined by moon phases and is related to the Jewish holiday of Passover, as Jesus was crucified around that time. The Council of Nicaea in 325 established the rule for determining Easter's date, which is the first Sunday after the first full moon following the vernal equinox. This rule can lead to two separate dates for Easter between Western and Orthodox Christians.

In the Holy Land, Easter was celebrated in Jerusalem's Church of the Holy Sepulcher, where Catholics and Armenian Christians marked the Resurrection. However, Eastern Orthodox Christians celebrated a week later due to their use of the Julian calendar. A blood moon appeared in the sky between Good Friday and Easter Sunday, which is not a coincidence, as the dates of both Passover and Easter are determined by moon phases.

In Europe and the United States, Easter traditions have evolved, including the use of eggs and the Easter bunny. German immigrants brought the bunny to North America in the 1700s, and the tradition of coloring eggs dates back to the 17th century. A unique method for coloring eggs using Kool-Aid has been suggested by a YouTube science geek, which produces bright colors without the smell of vinegar.

The Pope, in his Urbi et Orbi address, expressed hope for an end to violence and suffering in conflicts around the world, and he repeated the Biblical account of a woman washing Jesus' feet. Easter is a time for Christians to celebrate the Resurrection and to reflect on the values of compassion and love.

Japanese Defense Minister Gen Nakatani stated that the country's Air Self Defense Force (ASDF) has never encountered an extraterrestrial unidentified flying object (UFO). He responded to a question from former wrestler-turned-lawmaker Antonio Inoki, who asked if aircraft were scrambled to meet extraterrestrial threats. Nakatani revealed that jets sometimes detect birds or other flying objects but have never found evidence of a UFO from outer space. Inoki, who has a history of unconventional behavior, claims to have seen a UFO with his own eyes but admitted that he doesn't know if aliens exist. This exchange is not the first time Japanese politicians have discussed the implications of alien visitors.

Lauren Hill, the 19-year-old Indiana woman who inspired the world with her fight against brain cancer, has passed away. Despite being diagnosed with a rare and inoperable brain tumor in 2013, Hill continued to pursue her dream of playing college basketball. With the help of Mount St. Joseph University, her school successfully petitioned the NCAA to move up its first game to accommodate her, and she scored the first two points and final layup in front of a sellout crowd. Hill's determination and positivity raised over $1.4 million for pediatric cancer research and inspired millions worldwide. She was remembered as an "unselfish angel" and "true definition of strength" by those who knew her. NBA great LeBron James and NCAA President Mark Emmert were among those who paid tribute to her legacy. Hill's principal, Bill Snyder, said she taught everyone to be positive and work together to overcome obstacles.

A 20-30 foot fiberglass boat fragment, suspected to be from Japan's 2011 tsunami, was towed to Oregon's Newport marina, containing yellowtail jack fish, normally found in Japanese waters, which will be taken to the Oregon Coast Aquarium for further study.

Richie Benaud, the former Australia cricket captain and legendary broadcaster, has died at the age of 84. Benaud was a record-breaking leg-spinner and captain who led Australia to a series of victories, never losing a series in his 28 Tests as captain. He was also a renowned commentator, known for his witty one-liners and insightful commentary that resonated far beyond Australia's shores.

Benaud spent more than four decades with the BBC, bringing the game to millions of British living rooms. He was a household name in the UK, and his commentary was often imitated but never replicated. Australian Prime Minister Tony Abbott described Benaud as a "cricket icon" and asked that flags fly at half-mast on the day of his funeral.

Current Australian captain Michael Clarke and former teammate Shane Warne paid tribute to Benaud, remembering him as a "legend" and a "gentleman." British Prime Minister David Cameron also expressed his condolences, saying he grew up listening to Benaud's commentary.

Benaud's passing has been met with an outpouring of tributes from the cricket world and beyond, with many hailing him as the "godfather of cricket." He will be remembered for his contributions to the game, both on and off the field.

Malala Yousafzai, a Pakistani education activist, has been honored by NASA astrophysicist Amy Mainzer. Mainzer named an asteroid after Malala, discovered in 2010, as it orbits the sun between Mars and Jupiter. The asteroid, 316201 Malala, is 4 kilometers in diameter and has a dark surface. Mainzer supports Malala's cause, stating that educating girls increases human potential and is crucial for solving global problems.

An explosion outside a bus station in Gombe, Nigeria, killed at least five people and injured over a dozen others. A woman left her explosives-laden handbag near a bus, pretending to wait for passengers. She then disappeared, and the bag exploded, setting the bus on fire. No group has claimed responsibility, but Boko Haram is the main suspect due to its history of attacks on bus stations and markets in the region. The attack follows Nigeria's presidential election, where opposition candidate Muhammadu Buhari vowed to crush Boko Haram.

US President Barack Obama attended the Summit of the Americas in Panama, where he had a historic handshake with Cuban President Raul Castro. However, the summit's success is not solely dependent on this moment. The US has been losing influence in the region to China, Russia, and Iran, and Obama needs to put on a strong performance to reverse the tide.

Recent summits have been marred by diplomatic and PR disasters, including the 2012 Cartagena summit, where Secret Service agents hired prostitutes and the US was criticized for its handling of the situation. Obama also faced criticism in 2009 when Venezuelan President Hugo Chavez outplayed him at a summit.

This time, Obama has come armed with a new Cuba policy, but the White House has also made a miscalculation with Venezuela, imposing sanctions on the repressive regime of Nicolas Maduro. This move has given Maduro a way to portray himself as a victim of the US, which could revive past tensions with Latin Americans.

Despite these challenges, Obama has an opportunity to explain to the people of Latin America that the US supports democracy, human rights, and the rule of law, which are goals shared by the region. By meeting with Cuban dissidents and emphasizing the US's commitment to these values, Obama can leave a lasting legacy in the region.

A CNN team accompanied a Unicef aid mission to Yemen's war-torn Sanaa Airport. The airport, once bombed, is now off-limits due to a no-fly zone and ongoing conflict between Houthi rebels and a Saudi-led coalition. Despite a brief ceasefire, hostilities are expected to resume. The Unicef team aims to deliver vital food and supplies to ease Yemen's worsening humanitarian crisis, affecting 15.9 million people, or nearly two-thirds of the population. Thousands have fled the country on evacuation flights, but many remain in need of assistance, relying on mercy missions like Unicef's to survive.

A woman who wishes to remain anonymous shared a personal experience of being groped on a crowded train in Mumbai at the age of 13. This traumatic event has left her with a lifelong phobia of trains and made her aware of the pervasive issue of street harassment in India. According to a study by We the People, 80% of women in Mumbai have experienced street harassment, primarily in crowded areas. The woman has since been working to encourage women to speak out against harassment, but notes that it's often met with shame, fear, and silence.

Despite the cultural barriers, recent cases in India have shown that speaking out can lead to change. A young employee reported her boss, Rajendra Pachauri, for harassment, leading to his resignation from the United Nations Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change. Another case involved the founder of a media company, Tarun Tejpal, who was arrested for sexually assaulting his employee. The woman's male colleagues supported her in reporting the incident.

The author emphasizes that women have the power to shift the culture around sexual harassment in India by speaking out and seeking support from allies. It's essential to acknowledge that harassment is unacceptable and to confront the cultural and systemic barriers that prevent women from reporting incidents. By speaking out, women can reclaim their power and create a world where they feel safe and empowered to live full lives.

Mount Everest climbers have resumed their ascent for this year's climbing season, following a deadly incident in 2014 that killed 16 Nepalis. To reduce risks, the route through the treacherous Khumbu Icefall has been changed to a central route that takes longer but is considered safer. 

Nepal has issued 347 permits this year, with 125 of them from last year's shortened season. The local Nepalese committee decided to return to the central route, which was used in the 1990s but abandoned in favor of a quicker route. This new path means climbers will have to cross more crevasses and use more vertical and horizontal ladders.

However, some companies are choosing to climb the northern route from China, which is less popular due to concerns of government closures. This shift has raised concerns among Nepali companies, as Nepal heavily relies on tourism dollars. Many Sherpas, who lead expeditions to feed their families, are hesitant to return to the summit due to the risks and the emotional toll on their families.

The article discusses the growing trend of individuals getting lab tests without a doctor's order, often encouraged by celebrities and entrepreneurs. Mark Cuban, owner of the Dallas Mavericks, advised people to get blood tests every three months, while Taylor Swift encouraged fans to remind their parents to get screening tests. This has led to a rise in self-testing, with laboratories offering walk-in and online services. 

However, the article argues that this trend may lead to more medical care, not better health. Abnormal results are common in healthy people, and doctors may feel pressured to chase down these results with more testing, which can lead to unnecessary procedures and treatment. Research has shown that excessive testing can lead to anxiety, complications, and over-treatment of minor abnormalities.

The article suggests that the freedom to test may not be as beneficial as it seems and that regulation and education are necessary to prevent the misuse of medical data. It notes that the Food and Drug Administration should focus on protecting people from "snake oil testing" and that the public needs to understand that medical data is not always useful for healthy individuals.

Canadian fighter jets conducted their first airstrike against ISIS in Syria, hitting a garrison near Raqqa. The strike was deemed successful, with the military confirming the aircraft and crew safely returned to base. It's unclear how many casualties were caused. This marks Canada's expanded involvement in the US-led coalition against ISIS, with Defense Minister Jason Kenney stating the strike demonstrates Canada's firm resolve to tackle terrorism.

Female quintuplets were born in Houston on April 8, making them the first set since 1969. Danielle Busby delivered the five girls, Ava, Hazel, Olivia, Parker, and Riley, via C-section at 28 weeks. The family is now a family of eight, including big sister Blayke. The parents credit God and the medical team for their successful delivery and are documenting their experience on their blog. Meanwhile, another family's reaction to twin daughters went viral after being kept secret from family and friends.

The US Justice Department has revised its policy for individuals on the no-fly list, allowing them to know why they're banned from commercial flights and giving them a chance to dispute their status. This change comes after a June federal court ruling that the old process violated the Fifth Amendment's guarantee of due process. The American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) is not satisfied with the revised policy, stating it doesn't provide "meaningful notice, evidence, and a hearing." Under the new policy, individuals will receive a detailed explanation of why they're on the list, with an option to request further information and dispute their status in writing. The ACLU plans to challenge the revised policy in court, claiming it falls short of constitutional requirements.

A Texas veterinarian, Dr. Kristen Lindsey, has sparked outrage after posting a photo on Facebook of herself smiling with an arrow through the head of a cat. Lindsey claimed it was her first bow kill and made a comment about being the "vet of the year." However, an animal rescuer believes the cat was actually a pet that went missing from an elderly couple. The clinic where Lindsey works has fired her, covered her name with duct tape, and publicly distanced itself from her actions. Lindsey is facing investigation and could face charges. Animal rights activists are pushing for charges and a $7,500 reward is being offered for evidence leading to her arrest and conviction.

A Baltimore mom, seen in a viral video, smacks and scolds her masked son after allegedly seeing him throwing rocks at police during the city's riots. She was praised by Police Commissioner Anthony Batts for taking charge of her child.

A devastating earthquake hit Nepal on Saturday, causing widespread destruction and loss of life. The main highway out of Kathmandu shows massive cracks and damage, making travel times longer and more challenging. In the small village of Ravi Opi, 30 kilometers east of Kathmandu, 90% of the houses are uninhabitable, and residents are too scared to move back inside due to aftershocks.

Local residents have shared their harrowing stories of survival. Maili Tamang, 62, lost her home and had to crawl out of the rubble after the wooden balcony collapsed. Her daughter-in-law was trapped and had to be transported to a nearby hospital. Mahesh Koiraba, 31, lost his 2-year-old daughter in the quake, and his family is now struggling to survive.

Aid has yet to reach many areas, and villagers are back to work in their fields out of necessity. The situation is dire, with families displaced and living in makeshift shelters. Osminda Koirale, a young woman, expressed her fear and uncertainty about the future, saying that no government support has been seen in their area. The region is remote, and it may take days to reach some villages, where the full extent of human loss is still unknown.

Jeremy Renner, who plays Hawkeye, showcased his singing talents on "The Tonight Show," performing an Ed Sheeran parody, "Thinking Out Loud," and joking about his other hidden skills, including playing the trombone and opening a pickle jar.

Olivia Munn joins the cast of "X-Men: Apocalypse" as Psylocke, a telepathic character, alongside James McAvoy, Michael Fassbender, and Jennifer Lawrence. Munn will play Betsy Braddock, the original Psylocke, before the character's complicated plot twist.

Stephen Hawking has partnered with Monty Python to recreate their 1983 song "Galaxy Song" for Record Store Day. The 7-inch single features Hawking singing in his signature computerized voice, while a video shows him zooming through space and delivering a lesson on the cosmos. This is not Hawking's first musical venture, having previously featured on Pink Floyd's "Talkin' Hawkin." The song is available for download and features a humorous exchange with scientist Brian Cox.

The article is a reflection on the 35th anniversary of the Miami riots in 1980, which was triggered by the acquittal of four police officers in the beating death of an unarmed motorcyclist. The author, who was 12 years old at the time, recalls the fear and shock she felt during the riots. She notes that the riots were similar to others that took place in the 1960s, including the Watts riots, the Newark riots, and the Detroit riots, which were often triggered by perceived unjust police action.

The author suggests that riots are not always purposeless and uncontrolled violence, but rather a response to systemic injustices and a desire for attention and change. She cites the words of Martin Luther King Jr., who said that riots are the language of the unheard.

The article also touches on the recent riots in Baltimore, which were sparked by the death of Freddie Gray in police custody. The author notes that the riots were largely quashed, but the voices of nonviolent protesters continue to be heard.

The author concludes by suggesting that riots can be a catalyst for change, and that nonviolent protests can be an effective way to bring about systemic reform. She cites the example of the Ferguson protests, which were largely peaceful and led to a Justice Department report that highlighted systemic racial bias in the police department.

Overall, the article is a nuanced and thoughtful reflection on the complexities of riots and social justice, and the role that nonviolent protests can play in bringing about change.
Israeli airstrikes in the occupied Golan Heights killed three militants allegedly trying to plant a bomb on the Israeli border, the military said, preventing a potential bombing attack.

Singapore's "Cheryl's birthday challenge" has gone viral after a TV host posted it on Facebook. The puzzle, meant for high school students, asks users to deduce Cheryl's birthday from a list of 10 dates based on a conversation between friends Albert and Bernard.

A severe HIV outbreak has been reported in rural Indiana, particularly in Scott and Jackson counties. Since mid-December, 142 people have tested positive for HIV, with 136 confirmed cases and six preliminary positive test results. The outbreak is linked to the use of the prescription opioid Opana, which is often injected multiple times a day, increasing the risk of needle sharing and infection. Health leaders attribute the rapid spread of the disease to the isolated rural area with sparse health resources and the lack of awareness about the danger of sharing needles. Education and needle exchange programs are being implemented to control the outbreak. Indiana University has set up a temporary clinic to provide treatment and testing, and health volunteers are going door-to-door to educate the population. The state has also declared a public health emergency and offered job services to affected individuals. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention warn that this outbreak should serve as a warning to remain vigilant against the spread of HIV and other infectious diseases.

A longtime friend of Joni Mitchell has filed a court petition to be named her conservator. Mitchell, a renowned singer-songwriter, was hospitalized after being found unconscious at home. The petition claims she's unconscious and unable to care for herself. However, Mitchell's website, approved by her friend Leslie Morris, states she's alert and expected to make a full recovery. The discrepancy has sparked confusion, with Mitchell's publicist confirming the website's statement is accurate.

A new book, "Clinton Cash: The Untold Story," by Peter Schweizer, is set to be released on May 5, raising questions about conflicts of interest involving big foreign donors to charities run by the Clinton family. The book is expected to prompt Team Clinton to focus on issues that voters care about, such as local jobs, rather than the potential conflicts. 

The Clinton Foundation received donations from the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, and Oman, among others, including Canada's foreign affairs department, which promoted the Keystone XL pipeline. The State Department's analysis of the pipeline's environmental impact was criticized, with some suggesting that the donation may have influenced the decision.

The Clinton Global Initiative was also criticized for partnering with banks under investigation or involved in litigation. However, there is no clear evidence of a direct exchange of money for favors. The book may not unveil new information, and voters may not prioritize the issue, according to a recent poll.

Clinton's charities have faced criticism for poor management, running deficits, and taking money from companies trying to curry favor. However, this is not new information, and voters may be more concerned about other issues, such as unemployment, schools, and taxes.
Michelle Keegan named sexiest woman in the world by FHM, beating Kendall Jenner, Jennifer Lawrence, Kate Upton, and Caroline Flack to the top spot.

Andrew Lesnie, the Oscar-winning cinematographer, has passed away at 59. He spent over a decade collaborating with Peter Jackson on the "Lord of the Rings" and "Hobbit" films, winning an Oscar for his work on "The Fellowship of the Ring." Lesnie also worked with Jackson on "King Kong" and "The Lovely Bones," and shot films such as "Rise of the Planet of the Apes" and "I Am Legend." He was known for balancing technology with artistic considerations, and was inducted into the Australian Cinematographers Society Hall of Fame in 2002. Peter Jackson and Russell Crowe, among others, have paid tribute to Lesnie, who suffered a heart attack on Monday.

In 2014, ambush attacks on police officers were the leading cause of felonious deaths in the line of duty for the fifth consecutive year. Despite this, Google continues to market a smartphone application, Waze, which allows users to locate police officers in real-time. This feature, known as "traffic cop," uses GPS navigation and crowdsourcing to alert users to traffic jams and the presence of law enforcement. While Google claims Waze is for the "common good," it poses a significant risk to police officers and deputies. The app's location feature was reportedly used by the assassin of two New York police officers in 2014. Google has refused to discuss concerns with law enforcement organizations, including the National Sheriffs' Association, despite its reputation as a responsible corporate citizen. The risks of Waze far outweigh its potential benefits, and Google should work with law enforcement to ensure the safety of both motorists and police officers.

A New York resident captured a rare quadruple rainbow in the early morning sky after a heavy rain. The picture went viral on Twitter, receiving hundreds of retweets. Experts say it's a double rainbow reflected off a smooth body of water, but the phenomenon has left people in awe, reminiscent of a famous 2010 double rainbow video with over 40 million views.

Photographer Simon Brann Thorpe's project "Toy Soldiers" aims to create a fresh perspective on war and conflict. In Western Sahara, a disputed region in northwestern Africa, Thorpe posed soldiers from the Polisario Front as green plastic figurines in the harsh desert landscape. This visual metaphor allows viewers to develop their own emotional and political response to war. Thorpe's project highlights the lack of media coverage on the Western Sahara conflict, which has been ongoing for over 40 years. The project took five weeks to complete, with Thorpe working with 50-60 soldiers at a time, and is now available in book form through Dewi Lewis Publishing.

A gunman entered Wayne Community College in Goldsboro, North Carolina, and fatally shot the school's print shop operator, Ron Lane. The suspect, 20-year-old Kenneth Morgan Stancil III, worked with the victim and is a former student. The school was placed on lockdown, and Stancil is considered "armed and dangerous." Authorities are working to apprehend him. The incident is described as an isolated situation, and the college's president praised the rapid response of law enforcement and first responders.

Colorado's New Belgium Brewery and Ben & Jerry's are collaborating on a beer inspired by salted caramel brownie ice cream. The project aims to raise awareness for social causes, aligning with both companies' histories of activism. The beer will hit shelves in the fall, with details on the campaign to be announced later this year. As "B Corporations," both companies prioritize sustainability and social responsibility. The partnership combines New Belgium's beers with Ben & Jerry's iconic ice cream flavors.

The Kentucky Wildcats' bid for perfection ended with a 71-64 loss to the Wisconsin Badgers in the NCAA men's basketball Final Four. Wisconsin will face Duke in the title game on Monday night after the Blue Devils dominated Michigan State 81-61. Frank Kaminsky led Wisconsin with 20 points and 11 rebounds, while Karl-Anthony Towns led Kentucky with 16 points. Wisconsin came back from a 60-56 deficit with 6:39 left in the game, going on an 8-0 run to regain the lead.

Duke's win over Michigan State was led by Freshman Justise Winslow with 19 points and National Freshman of the Year Jahlil Okafor with 18 points. Duke's defense was key in the game, with Coach Mike Krzyzewski praising its performance. Wisconsin's win over Kentucky was attributed to their ability to defend the Wildcats' big men and their strong rebounding, winning by 12. Wisconsin will look to win its first title since 1941, while Duke will aim to tie Indiana and North Carolina for third-most NCAA championships with a win on Monday night.

Saudi forces have resumed airstrikes in southern Yemen, despite calls from Houthi rebels for peace talks. The rebels are demanding a complete halt of attacks before negotiations can begin. The airstrikes, which started in March, are part of Operation Decisive Storm, a Saudi-led campaign to restore the Yemeni government, a key US ally in the fight against al Qaeda. The operation has been replaced by Operation Renewal of Hope, which focuses on the political process. However, the airstrikes resumed after rebel forces attacked a Yemeni government military brigade. The Houthis have released Yemeni Defense Minister Mahmoud al-Subaihi, who was detained in March. The UN has demanded his release. Saudi officials say the campaign has degraded Houthi-controlled military infrastructure and achieved its objectives through precise execution and bravery. The Saudi-led coalition aims to protect civilians, enhance humanitarian assistance, confront terrorism, and create an international coalition to provide maritime security. Houthi leader Abdul-Malik al-Houthi has stated that the rebels will not surrender, and that a peaceful resolution is unlikely.

Iraqi forces are fighting to hold off ISIS militants in the city of Ramadi, the capital of Anbar province, about 70 miles west of Baghdad. Deputy head of the Anbar Provincial Council, Falih Essawi, told CNN that government troops are under intense pressure and may not be able to hold their front lines for much longer. At least 10 Iraqi security forces were killed and over 100 wounded in the fighting on Wednesday.

Essawi, who was on the front line armed with a machine gun, begged the Iraqi government for reinforcements and the U.S.-led coalition for air support. He stated that urgent support is needed to save the city. The ISIS offensive has driven a steady stream of refugees out of Ramadi, with over 150,000 people fleeing since Wednesday morning.

The U.S. military has carried out airstrikes against ISIS targets near Ramadi, but ISIS fighters have made significant advances in the city. According to Essawi, ISIS militants have taken control of areas east of Ramadi, and are now rolling into the center of the city. The situation is dire, with residents fleeing on foot and the city's infrastructure under threat.

On Equal Pay Day, April 14, presidential candidate Hillary Clinton should make a significant announcement to draw attention to the wage gap between men and women in America. According to the calculation, women would have to work until April 14, 2015, to make the same amount of money that men made in 2014. The average woman loses $431,000 in pay over a 40-year career due to the 23% pay gap.

Clinton should announce that if elected president, she will take a 23% pay cut to stand in solidarity with working women in America. This symbolic gesture would show that she is committed to fixing the inequality and ensuring that all Americans are paid fairly. By taking a pay cut equivalent to the current gender wage gap, Clinton would be highlighting the issue and inspiring solutions.

This move would also demonstrate Clinton's willingness to put her money where her mouth is and show that she is a champion for the middle class, as she has stated in her campaign launch video. While some may see this as a political stunt, it can serve a noble purpose in highlighting an important problem and inspiring change.

ISIS and Boko Haram, two violent Islamist groups, have a unique strategy when it comes to treating women. While killing men is a tactic for winning battles and conquering territory, the treatment of women serves a different purpose - building a "caliphate" or a Sharia-ruled state. Women are not just victims of war but are being enslaved and incorporated into the daily life of territories they rule. 

ISIS and Boko Haram have a systematic approach to women, including forced marriage, sexual slavery, and conversion to Islam. The groups have targeted students, including the 276 kidnapped in Nigeria in 2014, and have forced them to move from house to house and village to village, preparing them for marriage to jihadis. 

The goal is to control women and use them to establish a functioning community, despite the brutal laws of the new society. Women are viewed as the property of men, but they are also needed to keep the home, raise children, and maintain social structures. 

The treatment of women by ISIS and Boko Haram is not just about sadism but is a methodical approach to establishing a new society. The groups have cited Islamic writings to justify their actions, including the selling of Yazidi prisoners as slaves. Muslim women in areas seized by Islamists have described oppressive and fear-filled lives, with many saying life is not worth living under such conditions.

SpaceX, a private space exploration company, is attempting to land a rocket on a floating platform in the ocean. Due to weather conditions, the initial launch was postponed to Tuesday at 4:10 p.m. ET from Cape Canaveral, Florida. The launch will carry an uncrewed cargo spacecraft, Dragon, to the International Space Station. After launch, SpaceX will try to land the bottom stage of the rocket on a drone ship in the Atlantic Ocean. Elon Musk aims to reduce costs by reusing rockets, similar to airplanes. If successful, SpaceX will master landing at sea and eventually on the ground.

In the Boston Marathon bombing trial, jurors have been deliberating for over seven hours but have not yet reached a verdict. Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, the 21-year-old accused bomber, faces life in prison or the death penalty. The trial has been emotionally wrenching, with jurors witnessing a video of the moment a bomb exploded, disemboweling an 8-year-old boy and ripping the leg off his sister.

Prosecutors have presented a compelling case, highlighting the horrors of the April 15, 2013, bombings, which killed three people and injured many others. They have shown the jury evidence of the brothers' alleged involvement, including a manifesto written by Dzhokhar Tsarnaev in which he expressed jealousy of his brother's death as a martyr.

The defense has maintained that Dzhokhar's older brother, Tamerlan Tsarnaev, was the instigator of the plot and that Dzhokhar was only following his lead. However, prosecutors argue that Dzhokhar was an equal partner in the crime and that he took an active role in planning and carrying out the bombings.

The jury has sent out two questions, which will be addressed when they return to court on Wednesday morning. The trial is expected to continue into a penalty phase if Tsarnaev is found guilty of at least one of the 17 capital counts.

A woman in Georgia, Ebony Dickens, posted a threatening message on Facebook under a fake name, calling for black people to shoot white police officers. The post, which included a specific threat to kill 15 police officers, was removed but not before authorities identified Dickens and obtained a search warrant for her home. A firearm and three computers were found, and Dickens was arrested and charged with disseminating information related to terrorist acts. She was released on a $10,000 bond after being banned from social media.

A recent discussion with journalism students from Kent State University has sparked concern about the decline of marriage in the United States. The students, all in their early twenties, expressed a lack of interest in getting married, citing the high cost of weddings and the importance of financial stability. One student, Jackie Demate, stated that she would rather be single and successful than in an unhappy marriage. This attitude is reflective of a larger trend, with 50% of respondents in a Pew Research report agreeing that society is just as well off without the emphasis on marriage and children.

Economists are concerned about the potential consequences of a decline in marriage, citing its correlation with economic well-being. However, the students interviewed emphasized the importance of love and partnership in a relationship, rather than the institution of marriage itself.

In contrast, Scandinavian countries such as Norway and Sweden have a high rate of unmarried couples, with 82% of couples in Norway having their first child out of wedlock. Despite this, these countries have high levels of well-being and quality of life, ranking high in the United Nations' quality-of-life survey.

Ultimately, the question of whether a society without marriage would be just as well off remains unclear. While some argue that marriage provides economic and social benefits, others see it as an outdated institution that is no longer necessary.

Iraqi forces, aided by Shiite militiamen, have taken control of the city of Tikrit from ISIS after a nine-month occupation. The city, birthplace of former dictator Saddam Hussein, was a key ISIS stronghold. Iraqi forces found vehicles laden with explosives and buildings that might be booby-trapped, leading to cautious entries and controlled explosions. 

The liberation of Tikrit is seen as a significant victory for the Iraqi government, which had failed to retake the city multiple times before. However, concerns remain about the behavior of the Iranian-backed Shiite militiamen, who may take "scorched earth" reprisals against the Sunni population, exacerbating sectarian tensions. 

Prime Minister Haider al-Abadi arrived in Tikrit to claim the victory, and Interior Minister Mohammed al-Ghabban said the enemy has been defeated and the battle will soon end. The victory sets the stage for Iraqi forces to take back Mosul, Iraq's second-largest city, which is a key target in the fight against ISIS.

The International Committee of the Red Cross has called for a 24-hour ceasefire in Yemen, warning that many people wounded in airstrikes and ground fighting will die if not treated soon. Blaze Pizza is a local business located at 6546 Pardall Rd, Goleta, CA, offering a variety of options including pizza, gluten-free, salad, and fast food. The Live Oak Cafe is a local business located at 2220 Bath St in Santa Barbara, California. Winchell's Donuts is a local business located at 202 N Milpas in Santa Barbara, California. The Ritz-Carlton Bacara, Santa Barbara is a hotel and resort located at 8301 Hollister Ave in Santa Barbara, California. Campus Point Coffee is a local business located at 6560 Pardall Rd in Goleta, CA. It falls under the categories of Food, Cafes, Coffee & Tea, Bakeries, and Restaurants. The Social Security Administration has announced a 3.2% increase in monthly benefits for over 66 million retirees in 2024. This cost-of-living adjustment aims to help retirees keep up with rising living expenses. The average monthly benefit will increase by over $50, starting in January. The maximum Social Security tax earnings limit will rise to $168,600 in 2024. Beneficiaries will receive notices of the increase in early December. This 3.2% COLA is lower than last year's 8.7% but higher than the 20-year average of 2.6%.

Pittsburgh artist Tonee Turner, 22, went missing on December 30, 2019. She was last seen at Dobra Tea in the city. Her family has been searching for her, passing out flyers and gathering information. Tonee's purse was found near a bridge in Pennsylvania, containing her phone, wallet, and keys. Authorities believe she may have traveled on Interstate 80. Turner is 5'3", with black or dark brown hair and multiple piercings. If you have any information, contact the Pittsburgh Police at 412-323-7800.

Xanax, a benzodiazepine medication, is commonly prescribed for anxiety but its effectiveness is debated. It works by enhancing GABA, a calming neurotransmitter, providing quick relief for acute anxiety episodes. However, long-term use can lead to tolerance and dependence. For chronic anxiety, other treatments like therapy and lifestyle modifications may be more effective. A holistic approach is recommended, incorporating various strategies under the guidance of a healthcare professional.

Hannah Rose, a Survivor 45 castaway, revealed why she quit the show in a new exit interview. She stated that she couldn't handle the extreme hunger and lack of basic necessities, such as a flint, pot, and machete, in the early stages of the game. Hannah's tribe was forced to live without these essentials, making it difficult for her to find nourishment and rest. She mentioned that she didn't sleep at all during her time on the show, and the lack of sleep made it hard for her to keep her energy levels up. US troops from Fort Cavazos in Killeen and Fort Bliss in El Paso, Texas, are deploying to the Middle East to protect US forces from drone and rocket attacks. The deployment comes after at least 12 attacks on US and coalition troops in Iraq and Syria. Approximately 900 US troops will be deployed, including those from Texas, with a focus on manning THAAD and Patriot missile defense systems for regional deterrence efforts. 21 US forces have suffered minor injuries, mostly traumatic brain injuries, in the recent attacks.

In Big Brother 25, the house wants HOH Bowie Jane to backdoor Cameron Hardin, considering him a competition threat. However, Bowie has different plans and put Felica and Cirie on the block instead. Elle Marketing Events is offering a $20,000 marketing services grant to small business owners. The grant provides high-level consulting and support for businesses seeking growth opportunities. Applications are open until October 31 and three additional $500 consulting grants will also be awarded. To be eligible, businesses must have at least two years of history, be based in the US, and have the primary owner as the decision-maker.

New York House Republicans have made a motion to expel Representative George Santos from Congress due to 23 new federal criminal counts, including identity theft and unauthorized credit card charges. The motion claims Santos is "not fit to serve" and cites past allegations of resume fabrication. A vote will occur this week, but Santos may be spared due to Republicans' narrow majority, potentially allowing leadership to table the measure or refer it to a committee.

Survivor host Jeff Probst has clarified the sit-out rule for contestants. In the past, castaways couldn't sit out consecutive challenges, but a loophole allowed them to do so within a single cycle. However, with the shortened season length, this created an issue where one person frequently sat out. The new rule states that if someone sits out of a challenge, they must participate in the next one. This change was prompted by complaints from fans, including a situation in Season 44 where contestant Claire Rafson sat out three consecutive Immunity Challenges.

On 'The Young and the Restless', Nick Newman forces Sally Spectra to choose between him and Adam Newman. After learning Sally has unresolved feelings for Adam, Nick breaks up with her, urging her to sort out her feelings. Sally is torn between the brothers, with strong connections to both. She and Adam have a romantic encounter, but she still cares for Nick. Nick demands Sally make a decision, leading to a physical altercation with Adam. Sally's choice will be a shock to viewers.

A team of scientists at Rice University received $45 million to develop an implant called HAMMR, which can monitor cancer and adjust immunotherapy doses in real-time. The implant is a three-inch device that delivers immunotherapy drugs via a closed-loop system, potentially eradicating cancer in 60 days. The first clinical trial will focus on recurrent ovarian cancer, with human trials expected to begin within five years. This technology holds promise for treating a range of peritoneal cancers.

The Miami Dolphins are seeking to strengthen their defense ahead of the trade deadline. Despite a strong performance against the Philadelphia Eagles, the team's defensive line has struggled to generate consistent pressure. With needs in areas such as the offensive line and defense, the Dolphins are reportedly interested in acquiring Washington Commanders' defensive end Chase Young. Young, who has 5 sacks this season, would be a significant upgrade over the Dolphins' current options, including Emmanuel Ogbah, who has only 2.5 sacks this season.

A 1988 Georgia cold case has been solved using genealogy technology. Chong Un Kim, a 26-year-old Korean immigrant, was identified as the victim found in a Jenkins County dumpster. Kim had been deceased for 4-7 days due to asphyxiation. The GBI initially failed to identify Kim through DNA technology, but collaboration with a Texas-based company, Othram, Inc., led to a breakthrough in 2023. Kim's family was notified in October 2023. The GBI is now seeking information from anyone who may have known Kim or has information related to the case.

On Big Brother 25, the final five houseguests played for Head of Household (HOH) after a double eviction. The feeds went down for most of Thursday evening, but when they turned back on, Matt Klotz was shown with the HOH key. This is Matt's first time being HOH this season. Matt has a difficult decision to make, considering his alliances with Jag and Felicia. With only two weeks left, each houseguest has played for 86 days.

Usher's ex-wife Tameka Raymond participated in a fireside chat with Ariel Shaw, MBA, hosted by Southern Crescent Women In Business. The event allowed attendees to learn about Tameka's role as a businesswoman, mother, and philanthropist. She discussed balancing motherhood and entrepreneurship, her philanthropic work through The Kile's World Foundation, and her memoir "Here I Stand...In A Beautiful State." The event included a book signing and photo opportunities. Sponsors included Southern Crescent Women in Business and other local companies. Tameka's memoir explores themes of growth and resilience.

The US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) agency will continue processing work permits for migrants even if the federal government shuts down. To speed up the process, USCIS has taken steps including education sessions, email alerts, and mobile biometric services. Director Jaddou aims to complete work permit applications within a 30-day window on average. However, she requests more funding from Congress to process more applications efficiently.

China has launched its first nuclear-powered guided missile submarines, enhancing its power projection capabilities. The Pentagon warns this means China can conduct long-range precision strikes against land targets from its submarines and surface combatants. This development is concerning, especially given China's plans to nearly double its nuclear warheads to 1000 by 2030 and expand its navy to 435 ships and submarines by 2030. The US military is closely observing these developments, which come as China's rhetoric against Taiwan intensifies.

The Social Security Administration announced a 3.2% increase in benefits for 71 million Americans receiving Social Security in 2024. This translates to a $59 monthly increase for retired workers, bringing their average monthly benefit to $1,907. Although higher than typical, it's lower than last year's 8.7% increase. The rise helps retirees with lower and middle incomes maintain buying power, but rising Medicare Part B premiums may offset some gains. A looming funding shortfall and debate over the cost-of-living adjustment calculation method also pose concerns for the program's long-term stability.

Wardi McDonald, 34, vanished from Detroit, Michigan on February 1, 2001. Her siblings were the last to see her, but details of her disappearance remain a mystery. She is listed as an endangered missing person, but the reason for this classification is unclear. Wardi is described as 5'3"-5'4" with brown hair, brown eyes, and distinctive features. Her life and disappearance have been largely unknown, and authorities are seeking information to help solve her case.

The US Air Force has deployed an additional squadron of F-16 Fighting Falcons to the Middle East for hostility deterrence. The 119th Expeditionary Fighter Squadron from the New Jersey Air National Guard, also known as the "Jersey Devils," will play a crucial role in maintaining stability and security in the region. The deployment aims to enhance the military's capabilities and readiness in response to escalating tensions. This move is part of a broader effort to bolster the American presence in the area and collaborate with allies to resolve the conflict between Israel and Hamas.

A Texas judge, Alia Moses, granted a temporary restraining order, halting U.S. Customs and Border Patrol agents from cutting concertina wire on the southern border. The order is until November 13. The move comes after Attorney General Ken Paxton sued the Biden administration, saying the wire was being cut to allow migrants to enter Texas. The Biden administration claims the wire was cut for medical aid. The case will be argued on November 7.

Illinois Senate President Don Harmon is at the center of a controversy over tax legislation benefiting nursing homes in Cook County. He accepted nearly $2 million in campaign contributions from the nursing home industry, with over $700,000 received in the past year. The legislation, which Harmon supports, would reclassify nursing homes as residential property, lowering their property taxes by millions. Despite Governor J.B. Pritzker's veto, citing concerns about shifting the financial burden onto suburban homeowners, the Health Care Council and nursing homes are seeking legislative support to override the veto. Harmon's office has not commented on the contributions or his stance.

On this day in Minnesota history, Rosalie Wahl was appointed as the state's first female Supreme Court justice in 1977. Wahl, a pioneering woman, dedicated her life to justice, championing gender fairness, racial equality, and the rights of the underserved. Born in 1924 in Kansas, Wahl studied sociology at the University of Kansas and later attended law school in Minnesota, becoming an assistant public defender before her appointment to the bench. During her tenure, Wahl led task forces on gender fairness and racial bias, writing 549 opinions that emphasized the implementation of legislative will. Her legacy continues to inspire the pursuit of justice, emphasizing empathy and the rights of all individuals.

A pregnant worker in Georgia was fired from her Dollar General job after informing her manager of her pregnancy in 2020. The US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) sued Dollar General, leading to a $42,500 settlement. The EEOC emphasizes that pregnancy shouldn't be a reason to assume an employee can't work, citing federal laws protecting pregnant employees from discrimination. The case highlights the importance of protecting pregnant employees' rights and preventing detrimental stereotypes in the workplace.

JetBlue is cutting 14 routes from major hubs, including New York, Boston, and Los Angeles, starting in January and continuing into March. The decision is influenced by the dissolution of the Northeast Alliance with American Airlines and ongoing Air Traffic Control staffing challenges. Impacted cities include Newark, Miami, Nashville, and Washington DC, among others. Passengers booked on these routes will receive alternative flights or refunds. The majority of discontinued routes involve John F. Kennedy International, LaGuardia, and Boston Logan airports.

A former FBI agent, David Paitsel, and D.C. real estate developer, Brian Bailey, were sentenced for their roles in a bribery scheme involving unauthorized sharing of confidential data from the D.C. Department of Housing and Community Development. Paitsel received 24 months in prison, while Bailey was sentenced to 48 months and a $250,000 fine. Dawne Dorsey, a program specialist, pleaded guilty in June 2019 and awaits sentencing.

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro's office settled a sexual harassment claim against a senior aide, Mike Vereb, for $295,000. The former employee accused Vereb of making lewd comments and facing retaliation. As part of the settlement, the governor's office will provide harassment training and allow the woman to seek employment elsewhere in state government. The case highlights the importance of creating a respectful culture in government and beyond.

Texas Governor Greg Abbott condemned the attack on Israel, denouncing it as "heinous acts of violence" and "terrorism." He increased security at Jewish and Israel-related locations, directed the Texas Department of Public Safety to provide support, and restricted Texas agencies from purchasing goods tied to Hamas. Abbott also distributed $4 million in grant funding to 31 Jewish organizations to boost their security. The Texas flag will be flown at half-staff in honor of those who lost their lives, including American citizens.

Mainers can expect a nationwide phone alert on Wednesday, October 4, at 2:20 p.m. EDT (various times across time zones). The alert is a test of the Emergency Alert System, conducted by FEMA to ensure its reliability and efficiency. Phones will display a clear message stating "this is a test" in English and Spanish. The test is part of a routine evaluation, last conducted in 2021. Some exceptions include phones off, in airplane mode, or out of cell tower range, or older phones.

Reese Moore, a senior from Tishomingo County High School, signed with Freed-Hardeman University. California Governor Gavin Newsom and First Partner Jennifer Siebel Newsom are embarking on a weeklong trip to China, focusing on climate action and economic development. The trip aims to advance climate initiatives, boost tourism, and encourage cultural exchange. The governor will visit five cities, including Hong Kong, Shenzhen, Guangzhou, Beijing, and Shanghai. He will engage in discussions on climate collaboration, electric vehicle transition, and economic growth, and meet with regional leaders and businesses. The trip is seen as crucial ahead of the APEC Summit in San Francisco this November, aiming to solidify the partnership between California and China, two of the world's largest economies.

Melissa Claire Egan, the actress who plays Chelsea on The Young and the Restless, has returned to filming after maternity leave. She welcomed her second son in July and is now back on set. Kogilicious is a Korean restaurant located at 956 Embarcadero Del Norte in Isla Vista, CA. It is open seven days a week from 10:00 AM to 11:00 PM. Customers can park on the street and enjoy their meal outside, as the restaurant offers outdoor seating.

Dargan's Irish Pub & Restaurant is a local eatery located at 18 E Ortega St in Santa Barbara, CA. This gastropub offers a variety of services, including restaurants, bars, and nightlife. Uncorked Wine Tasting and Kitchen is a wine bar and restaurant located at 432 E Haley St, Santa Barbara, CA. Sushi Ai, located at 7020 Marketplace Dr in Goleta, CA, offers a variety of sushi and Japanese dishes. Minnow Cafe is a local eatery located at 9 Breakwater in Santa Barbara, California. Celebration Cruises, located at 237 Stearns Wharf in Santa Barbara, California, offers a variety of services including boat charters, whale watching tours, and event planning. The business operates on a daily basis from 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM, Monday through Sunday.
